```{r setup}
#| echo: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(ggplot2)
})
source("../R/helpers.R")   # bind_part()

T1 <- readRDS("fresh_dich_null.rds")     # tier 1, null, B to 10 000
T2 <- readRDS("fresh_dich_misfit.rds")   # tier 2, k = 1 and 3, B to 2000
s_grid <- readRDS("../simulations/infit_width_iterations_S2.rds")  # submitted Study 2
s_conv <- readRDS("../simulations/infit_width_iterations_S1.rds")  # submitted Study 1
AL <- 0.05
WIDTHS <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99, 0.995, 0.999)
```

The design is in `rerun_plan.md` and the code in `fresh_rerun.R`. Both
dichotomous studies of the submission are regenerated with fresh data in every
replication, using the same 20 item locations and misfitting items. Each
replication runs one bootstrap at the largest B, and every smaller B uses its
first B draws. Comparisons with the submission use the cached results of
Studies 1 and 2, which drew every sample from one master dataset per condition.

# Integrity

```{r integrity}
keys <- c("rep", "k", "n")
P1 <- bind_part(T1, "pval", keys) |> mutate(cell = paste(rep, k, n))
H1 <- bind_part(T1, "hdci", keys) |> mutate(cell = paste(rep, k, n))
P2 <- bind_part(T2, "pval", keys) |> mutate(cell = paste(rep, k, n))
H2 <- bind_part(T2, "hdci", keys) |> mutate(cell = paste(rep, k, n))

short_draws <- bind_rows(P1 |> mutate(tier = 1), P2 |> mutate(tier = 2)) |>
  distinct(tier, cell, B, B_used) |>
  filter(B_used < B) |>
  summarise(n_short = n(), max_missing = max(B - B_used), .by = tier)

data.frame(
  tier = 1:2,
  cells = c(nrow(T1$grid), nrow(T2$grid)),
  failed = c(sum(vapply(T1$res, is.null, logical(1))),
             sum(vapply(T2$res, is.null, logical(1)))),
  hours = round(c(T1$elapsed_min, T2$elapsed_min) / 60, 2),
  na_pvalues = c(sum(is.na(P1$padj_fwer)), sum(is.na(P2$padj_fwer)))
) |>
  left_join(short_draws, by = "tier") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

All cells completed and no p-value is missing. Where a refit failed inside a
bootstrap, the largest B used the draws that succeeded, and the table shows how
many replication-by-B combinations were affected and by how many draws at most.

```{r long}
# One row per replication, B, item and rule
long_rules <- function(P, H) {
  P <- P |>
    mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"),
           p_bonf = p.adjust(p_marg, "bonferroni"),
           .by = c(cell, B))
  lab <- c(p_marg = "Marginal", p_bonf = "Bonferroni", p_holm = "Holm",
           padj_fwer = "Westfall-Young", padj_bh = "Benjamini-Hochberg",
           p_marg_pool = "Marginal, joint", padj_fwer_pool = "Westfall-Young, joint")
  LP <- P |>
    select(cell, rep, k, n, B, item, all_of(names(lab))) |>
    pivot_longer(all_of(names(lab)), names_to = "rule", values_to = "p") |>
    mutate(rule = unname(lab[rule]), flag = as.integer(p < AL)) |>
    select(-p)
  LH <- H |>
    transmute(cell, rep, k, n, B, item,
              rule = sprintf("Interval %.3f", w), flag = as.integer(code > 0))
  bind_rows(LP, LH)
}
mis_of <- function(k) T1$items$mis[seq_len(k)]
stopifnot(identical(T1$items$mis, s_grid$misfit))   # same misfitting items
L1 <- long_rules(P1, H1) |> mutate(is_mis = FALSE)
L2 <- long_rules(P2, H2) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% mis_of(k), k, item))

per_rep <- function(L, by) {
  L |>
    summarise(n_fp = sum(flag[!is_mis]), n_tp = sum(flag[is_mis]),
              n_mis = sum(is_mis), n_fit = sum(!is_mis),
              .by = all_of(c(by, "cell", "B", "rule"))) |>
    mutate(any_fp = as.integer(n_fp > 0),
           fdp = ifelse(n_fp + n_tp > 0, n_fp / (n_fp + n_tp), 0))
}
summ <- function(L, by) {
  per_rep(L, by) |>
    summarise(R = n(),
              Det = 100 * sum(n_tp) / sum(n_mis),
              FP = 100 * sum(n_fp) / sum(n_fit),
              FWER = 100 * mean(any_fp),
              se = 100 * sd(any_fp) / sqrt(n()),
              FDR = 100 * mean(fdp),
              .by = all_of(c(by, "B", "rule")))
}
```

# E4: Table 4 extended to B = 10 000

```{r tbl4}
#| tbl-cap: "Familywise error under the null, 20 dichotomous items, pooled over n (2 000 replications per B)"
S1 <- summ(L1, character(0))
S1 |>
  filter(rule %in% c("Marginal", "Bonferroni", "Holm", "Westfall-Young",
                     "Benjamini-Hochberg", "Westfall-Young, joint")) |>
  select(B, rule, FWER) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = FWER) |>
  rename(Marg = Marginal, Bonf = Bonferroni, WY = `Westfall-Young`,
         BH = `Benjamini-Hochberg`, `WY joint` = `Westfall-Young, joint`) |>
  arrange(B) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r tbl4-se}
#| include: false
se_wy <- max(S1$se[S1$rule == "Westfall-Young"])
```

Binomial standard errors are at most `r sprintf("%.2f", se_wy)` points per
cell. The submitted Table 4, from the master-dataset study with 1 000
replications per B, read 6.8, 5.2, 4.3, 4.2 and 3.8% for Westfall-Young at
B = 100 to 2000.

```{r wy-n}
#| tbl-cap: "Westfall-Young familywise error under the null by sample size: fresh data (500 per n) and the submitted master-dataset study (250 per n)"
fresh_n <- summ(L1, "n") |> filter(rule == "Westfall-Young") |>
  mutate(data = "fresh")
master_n <- bind_part(s_grid, "pval", keys) |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  summarise(any = any(padj_fwer < AL), .by = c(rep, n, B)) |>
  summarise(FWER = 100 * mean(any), .by = c(n, B)) |>
  mutate(data = "master")
bind_rows(fresh_n |> select(data, n, B, FWER), master_n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = B, values_from = FWER, names_prefix = "B = ") |>
  arrange(data, n) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

**Summary for E3.** The rise at n = 1000 is gone in fresh data. The submitted
Westfall-Young null rate at n = 1000 was 5.6 to 9.2% across B, against 3.8 to
6.0% in the rerun, and from B = 400 the fresh rate at n = 1000 (3.8 to 4.2%) is
in the range of the other sample sizes (2.2 to 5.0%). The rise was a property of
the master dataset for that condition, as suspected, and not of the sample
size. Pooled over sample sizes, the master-dataset study was higher at every common
B, by 0.3 to 1.2 points (5.6% against 6.8% at B = 100, 3.5% against 3.8% at
B = 2000).

# R1.2: the studentization test

The joint variant studentizes the observed and simulated statistics by moments
computed over all B + 1 values, which removes the asymmetry that the
explanation in the letter points to. If the explanation is right, the joint
variant should show no excess at small B, and the two variants should agree at
large B.

```{r joint}
#| tbl-cap: "Westfall-Young under the null, standard against joint studentization, paired within replication"
pair_j <- per_rep(L1 |> filter(rule %in% c("Westfall-Young", "Westfall-Young, joint")),
                  character(0)) |>
  select(cell, B, rule, any_fp) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = any_fp) |>
  mutate(d = `Westfall-Young` - `Westfall-Young, joint`) |>
  summarise(R = n(),
            standard = 100 * mean(`Westfall-Young`),
            joint = 100 * mean(`Westfall-Young, joint`),
            diff = 100 * mean(d), se_diff = 100 * sd(d) / sqrt(n()),
            .by = B) |>
  arrange(B)
pred <- data.frame(B = sort(unique(P1$B))) |>
  mutate(c = qnorm(1 - (1 - 0.95^(1 / 20)) / 2),
         predicted = 100 * (1 - (1 - 2 * pt(-c, B - 1))^20)) |>
  select(-c)
left_join(pair_j, pred, by = "B") |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r marg-item}
#| tbl-cap: "Per-item rejection rate of the marginal p-value under the null (percent of item tests), standard against joint"
attain <- function(B) 100 * floor(AL * (B + 1) - 1e-9) / (B + 1)
L1 |>
  filter(rule %in% c("Marginal", "Marginal, joint")) |>
  summarise(rate = 100 * mean(flag), .by = c(B, rule)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = rate) |>
  mutate(`attainable size` = attain(B)) |>
  arrange(B) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The last column is the largest rejection probability a valid Monte Carlo test
can have at that B, since p-values take the values $j/(B + 1)$ and $p < .05$
admits only those below .05.

```{r fig-joint}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Westfall-Young familywise error under the null against B, 20 dichotomous items, fresh data"
fig_d <- bind_rows(
  pair_j |> transmute(B, value = standard, what = "Standard studentization"),
  pair_j |> transmute(B, value = joint, what = "Joint studentization"),
  pred |> transmute(B, value = predicted, what = "Predicted, t asymmetry")
) |>
  mutate(what = factor(what, c("Standard studentization", "Joint studentization",
                               "Predicted, t asymmetry")))
ggplot(fig_d, aes(B, value, linetype = what, shape = what)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = sort(unique(P1$B)),
                labels = format(sort(unique(P1$B)), big.mark = " ")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 1, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B), log scale", y = "Familywise error (%)",
       linetype = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Summary for E4 and R1.2.** The explanation is confirmed on the same draws.
With standard studentization the Westfall-Young rate was 5.6% at B = 100, 4.2%
at 200 and between 3.4 and 3.8% from 400 to 10 000. With joint studentization
it was 3.5% at B = 100 and between 3.1 and 3.6% at every B. The paired
difference was 2.05 points at B = 100 (SE 0.32), 1.05 at 200 (SE 0.23), 0.45 at
400 (SE 0.15), and 0.1 or less from 1000. The whole decline with B is therefore
the studentization asymmetry, and joint studentization removes it. The
t-based prediction gets the direction and the order of the decline right but
understates its size at B = 100 (a predicted excess of 1.3 points over the
large-B value against an observed 2.2).

What remains is a level, not a trend. Both variants settle at about 3.4%,
below the nominal 5%, and the rate does not move between B = 2000 and
10 000. The per-item marginal tests show the same thing at their own level,
rejecting 4.6 to 4.8% of fitting items against an attainable 5.0% at every B. A
conservatism that does not depend on B cannot be Monte Carlo error. It belongs
to the parametric bootstrap itself, whose reference distribution comes from
estimated parameters (the composite null of R1.2). The polytomous studies were
closer to nominal (4.2 to 5.0% from B = 400 in the cached results), so the
size of the conservatism depends on the item format or set.

Consequences. The letter's E4 and R1.2 responses can state the explanation as
tested rather than proposed. Joint studentization makes the first step of the
step-down an exact Monte Carlo test with respect to the fitted model, and in
these data it made the error rate independent of B from B = 100. That is a
candidate change for easyRasch2 (a decision outside this revision), and it would
mean the 400-iteration floor is needed for reproducibility rather than for
calibration.

# E3 and Study 1: interval convergence from fresh data

Width relative to the width at B = 10 000 of the same bootstrap, median over
items and replications, as in the submission (which used a separate bootstrap
at 10 000 iterations and 30 replications per n).

```{r conv}
relw_f <- H1 |>
  mutate(width = hi - lo) |>
  summarise(v = median(width), .by = c(n, w, B)) |>
  mutate(rel = v / v[B == max(B)], .by = c(n, w))
CV <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_conv$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_conv$res[[i]]
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  cbind(rep = s_conv$grid$rep[i], n = s_conv$grid$n[i], r)
}))
relw_m <- CV |>
  summarise(v = median(width), .by = c(n, w, B)) |>
  mutate(rel = v / v[B == max(B)], .by = c(n, w))
b99 <- function(relw) relw |>
  summarise(m = median(rel), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  summarise(B99 = min(B[m >= 0.99]), .by = w)
spread <- function(relw) relw |>
  summarise(sp = max(rel) - min(rel), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  summarise(mx = max(sp)) |> pull(mx)
```

```{r conv-tbl}
#| tbl-cap: "Median relative interval width (median over sample sizes), fresh data"
relw_f |>
  summarise(rel = median(rel), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = B, values_from = rel, names_prefix = "B = ") |>
  select(-`B = 10000`) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r conv-cmp}
#| tbl-cap: "Iterations reaching 99% of the reference width, and the largest spread between sample sizes"
left_join(b99(relw_f) |> rename(`B99 fresh` = B99),
          b99(relw_m) |> rename(`B99 submitted` = B99), by = "w") |>
  knitr::kable()
data.frame(data = c("fresh", "submitted"),
           max_spread_between_n = c(spread(relw_f), spread(relw_m))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**Summary for Study 1.** The convergence results replicate in fresh data. The
iterations needed to reach 99% of the reference width are the same as
submitted for every width (1000 for .90 and .95, 2000 for .99 and .995, 5000 for
.999), the .999 interval reaches 0.76 of the reference at B = 100 as before,
and the largest spread between sample sizes is smaller (0.008 against 0.018),
with 500 replications per n instead of 30. The reference is now B = 10 000 of
the same bootstrap rather than a separate one, which the Method must say.

# Interval rule under the null against Equation 1

```{r fwe-int}
#| tbl-cap: "Familywise error of the interval rule under the null (percent), fresh data, with the Equation 1 prediction"
S1 |>
  filter(grepl("^Interval", rule)) |>
  mutate(w = as.numeric(sub("Interval ", "", rule))) |>
  select(w, B, FWER) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = B, values_from = FWER, names_prefix = "B = ") |>
  mutate(pred = 100 * (1 - w^20)) |>
  arrange(w) |>
  mutate(w = sprintf("%.3f", w)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r fwe-int-master}
#| tbl-cap: "The same, submitted master-dataset study (Table 8, dichotomous rows)"
bind_part(s_grid, "hdci", keys) |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  summarise(any = any(code > 0), .by = c(rep, n, B, w)) |>
  summarise(FWER = 100 * mean(any), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = B, values_from = FWER, names_prefix = "B = ") |>
  mutate(pred = 100 * (1 - w^20)) |>
  arrange(w) |>
  mutate(w = sprintf("%.3f", w)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

**Summary.** The interval rule behaves as submitted. At w = .999 its familywise
error was 30.1% at B = 100, 7.7% at 400 and 2.6% at 2000, against 29.7, 8.6 and
2.9% submitted, and it reaches 1.6% at 10 000, against the Equation 1
prediction of 2.0%. At B = 10 000 every width is at or below its prediction
(ratios 0.80 to 0.98), consistent with mild positive dependence and with the
conservatism found for the p-value rules. For widths .90 to .99 at B = 2000 the
ratio of observed to predicted was 0.98 to 0.99.

# Study 2 misfit conditions from fresh data

## The detection and false positive trade-off (section 4.3)

```{r tradeoff}
#| tbl-cap: "Interval at w = .999, three misfitting items, n = 150: detection and per-item false positives by B"
trade <- function(L) L |>
  filter(k == 3, n == 150, rule == "Interval 0.999") |>
  summarise(Det = 100 * mean(flag[is_mis]), FP = 100 * mean(flag[!is_mis]),
            .by = B) |> arrange(B)
art_m <- bind_part(s_grid, "hdci", keys) |>
  filter(k == 3, n == 150, abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(is_mis = item %in% s_grid$misfit) |>
  summarise(Det = 100 * mean(code[is_mis] > 0), FP = 100 * mean(code[!is_mis] > 0),
            .by = B) |> arrange(B)
left_join(trade(L2), art_m, by = "B", suffix = c(" fresh", " submitted")) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r k1}
#| tbl-cap: "Interval at w = .999, one misfitting item, n = 150: detection by B"
L2 |>
  filter(k == 1, n == 150, rule == "Interval 0.999", is_mis) |>
  summarise(Det = 100 * mean(flag), .by = B) |> arrange(B) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

## Reachability sequences (section 5.1)

```{r reach}
#| tbl-cap: "Detection by B at n = 150, fresh data"
summ(L2 |> filter(n == 150), "k") |>
  filter(rule %in% c("Holm", "Westfall-Young", "Benjamini-Hochberg")) |>
  select(k, rule, B, Det) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = B, values_from = Det, names_prefix = "B = ") |>
  arrange(k, rule) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

The submission reported, at n = 150, Benjamini-Hochberg detection of 0, 8, 98,
99 and 100% (one misfitting item) and 14, 71, 78, 79 and 80% (three), and
Westfall-Young detection of 100% and 74% at every B.

## Partial nulls: familywise error over fitting items and FDR (R1.1, R1.3)

```{r partial}
#| tbl-cap: "Familywise error over fitting items, fresh data, B = 2000"
S2 <- summ(L2, c("k", "n"))
show_rules <- c("Interval 0.999", "Marginal", "Holm", "Westfall-Young",
                "Benjamini-Hochberg")
S2 |>
  filter(B == 2000, rule %in% show_rules) |>
  select(k, n, rule, FWER) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = FWER) |>
  rename(Interval = `Interval 0.999`, WY = `Westfall-Young`,
         BH = `Benjamini-Hochberg`) |>
  arrange(k, n) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r fdr}
#| tbl-cap: "False discovery rate, fresh data, B = 2000"
S2 |>
  filter(B == 2000, rule %in% show_rules) |>
  select(k, n, rule, FDR) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = FDR) |>
  rename(Interval = `Interval 0.999`, WY = `Westfall-Young`,
         BH = `Benjamini-Hochberg`) |>
  arrange(k, n) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r holm-wy}
#| tbl-cap: "Westfall-Young minus Holm detection (points), paired within replication, B = 2000"
L2 |>
  filter(B == 2000, is_mis, rule %in% c("Holm", "Westfall-Young")) |>
  summarise(d = mean(flag), .by = c(k, n, cell, rule)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = d) |>
  mutate(diff = 100 * (`Westfall-Young` - Holm)) |>
  summarise(R = n(), gain = mean(diff), se = sd(diff) / sqrt(n()),
            .by = c(k, n)) |>
  arrange(k, n) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

**Summary for the misfit conditions.** Every conclusion the submission drew from
these conditions holds in fresh data, with levels a few points different.

- The trade-off of section 4.3 replicates. With three misfitting items at
  n = 150, interval detection at w = .999 fell from 83.9% at B = 100 to 66.5% at
  1000 (submitted 80.8 to 65.3%), while false positives fell from 4.2% to 0.5%
  (submitted 4.0 to 0.5%). With one misfitting item detection stayed at or above
  99.6%.
- The reachability sequences replicate. Benjamini-Hochberg detected 0, 6.8,
  99.6, 99.6 and 100% of the single misfitting item at B = 100 to 2000
  (submitted 0, 8, 98, 99, 100), and Holm shows the same floor, with 0% at
  B = 100 and 200. Westfall-Young was flat at 99.6 to 100% and 76.9 to 77.9%
  (submitted 100% and 74%).
- Holm and Westfall-Young detection differed by at most 1.3 points at B = 2000
  (SE 0.6).
- Strong control fails in fresh data as it did in the cached results. At
  n = 1000 the Westfall-Young rate over fitting items was 28.0% with one
  misfitting item and 96.8% with three (cached 37.6 and 92.8%), and the
  Benjamini-Hochberg FDR was 25.2% and 70.0% (cached 30.8 and 67.2%). This is the
  strong misfit of rho = .15, so these rates are higher than at the anchored
  level.
